title: Restraint of speech (ch. 6)
hookLine: silence is valued even in good talk

lines: A GOOD REPLY, READY TO GO.
cards: A meeting, a dinner table, a group chat. Someone says something, and there's a good reply ready on your tongue. Not a cruel one.
A true one, even a kind one. Then a beat passes, the moment moves on, and the reply never gets said. Was something lost?
A rule for monks would be expected to warn about bad words, and Benedict's does. But chapter six goes somewhere stranger: sometimes even good words are better left unsaid, for the sake of silence.

teach.h: TAKE HEED, THAT I SIN NOT WITH MY TONGUE.
teach.b: Benedict opens the chapter with a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "I said: I will take heed to my ways: that I sin not with my tongue." The psalm goes on to say the speaker held his peace, even from good things.

teach.h: EVEN GOOD WORDS, FOR SILENCE'S SAKE.
teach.b: If the psalmist kept back even good words for silence's sake, he reasons, how much more should we keep back the harmful ones. So silence isn't only a fence against sin; it's valued for itself.
Then he leans on Proverbs: talk a great deal, and you won't escape sin. And a sharper line: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue." Words aren't weightless.
They build people, and they break them. Next, a line about roles.

teach.h: THE TEACHER SPEAKS. THE DISCIPLE LISTENS.
teach.b: In the monastery, speaking and teaching belong to the teacher; being quiet and listening belong to the disciple. So when a monk needs something from his superior, he asks humbly, with respect.
And one kind of talk is shut out everywhere: coarse jokes and idle chatter meant only to get a laugh. Here's what's easy to miss. Benedict doesn't ban speaking.
Monks talk, ask, teach, sing the psalms aloud.
The chapter is about restraint, not total silence: a rationing of words, so the ones that do get said can carry weight.

teach.h: DEATH AND LIFE ARE IN THE POWER OF THE TONGUE.
teach.b: And a person who speaks less has more room to listen, to others and, Benedict would add, to God.

how: Benedictine communities keep times and places of quiet, and Catholic retreat houses often ask guests to keep silence for part or all of a retreat.

o: holding back words so the ones said carry weight
a ban on talking to anyone outside the monastery
a vow of total silence that monks keep for life

p: in the power of the tongue

s: chapter six bans monks from speaking at all
monks talk, ask, teach and sing. the chapter rations words; it doesn't forbid them.
Benedict says even good words are sometimes better left unsaid
following the psalm, he values silence even over good talk.
in the Rule, a monk with a question shouldn't ask it
he asks humbly and with respect; listening is the disciple's part.

games.q: you're a monk with a true, kind thing to say, but the room has fallen quiet. what does chapter six lean toward?
o: say it: good words should always be spoken.
sometimes let even a good word go, for the sake of silence.
say it, and add a joke to lighten the quiet.
games.why: Benedict reads the psalm this way: even good words are sometimes held back for silence's sake, and jokes meant only for laughs are shut out.

practice: Run an upcoming conversation through your mind, a call, a meeting, supper, and notice where you'd usually add more: the extra explanation, the joke to fill a pause, the point already made once.
Leave one of those out and let the pause stay a pause; then just sit in the quiet you have right now, with nothing to say to anyone. If you pray, let the silence itself be the prayer.

wordCard.voice: Restraint of speech. Not a vow of silence, but a habit of holding back, so that the words that remain carry weight. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the word in the chapter's title: holding back from speech.

carryVoice: Your line: fewer words. The ones you keep can carry more weight. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Psalm 38:2 (Douay numbering; Psalm 39:1 in Hebrew numbering)
